programGuide.title: Writing a program by hand
programGuide.intro: Programs — multi-week plans that step through your workouts, optionally tweaking sets/reps/rounds as weeks go by — can be built right in the app, from the + button on the Programs tab. This page is for the other way: writing one as YAML and importing the file, which is handy for drafting a long block on a real keyboard or sharing it with someone else.

ids.title: 1. Find your workout IDs
ids.body: A program points at workouts by their id, not their display name. A workout's id is set automatically from its name when you create it in Workouts: lowercased, with anything that isn't a letter or number turned into a single hyphen. So a workout named <c>"Calisthenics A"</c> has the id <c>calisthenics-a</c>.

write.title: 2. Write the program
write.body: Save this as a .yaml file, filling in your own workout ids:

fields.title: 3. Fields
fields.body:
• <c>id</c> — the program's own slug, hand-typed (lowercase-with-hyphens is conventional).
• <c>name</c> — what shows in the Programs list.
• <c>weeks</c> — a list; each entry needs a <c>week</c> number and a <c>workout</c> id, unless it's a rest day (see below).
• <c>notes</c> — optional freeform text shown on that week.
• <c>overrides</c> — optional, see below.

overrides.title: 4. Overrides (optional)
overrides.intro: Each entry targets exactly one exercise or one circuit block, by id, with a partial config patch using that exercise's/circuit's own field names:
overrides.body: An exercise override only makes sense for a single exercise block. A block override only works on a circuit that was given its own id in Workouts (the optional "Block ID" field when editing a circuit) — it patches the circuit's own <c>rounds</c>/rest fields, not one member's config. Overrides don't carry forward — repeat one in every later week you want it to keep applying to.

multiDay.title: 5. More than one session a week (optional)
multiDay.body: Add a freeform <c>day</c> label when two weeks share the same week number — e.g. a push/pull split:

restDays.title: 6. Rest days (optional)
restDays.body: A week entry with <c>rest_day: true</c> and no <c>workout</c> is a scheduled day off. It takes its place in the rotation, so Workouts shows a rest card instead of queuing a session — and it moves on by itself a day later. Nothing is logged, and it can carry a <c>notes</c> line but no <c>overrides</c>, since it runs nothing to override.
restDays.tail: Write out every day off you actually take, including the ones at the end of the week. Kettle counts a rest entry as one day, so a three-day week written as three entries rolls straight into the next week the day after your last session.

importIt.title: 7. Import it
importIt.body: Pick your file, review the summary, and merge. Programs merge by id: a new id gets added, but re-importing an id that already exists replaces that whole program — all its weeks — with what's in the file, it doesn't merge week-by-week. So to add or change one week, include the program's complete, up-to-date week list in the file you import, not just the changed week.

settings.unitsImperialNote: Weights show in pounds. They are still stored in kilograms, so your exported library reads the same everywhere.
settings.soundsNote: The countdown tick, the ding when the exercise changes, and the chime at a halfway mark. Kettle plays them even when your phone is on silent, so this is the only way to quiet them. Vibration is separate and stays on your phone's own settings.

settings.exportHistoryDetail_other: Share all {{count}} logged sessions as a single file.
settings.exportHistoryEmpty: Nothing logged yet — finish a session first.
settings.importLibraryDetail: Merge a .yaml file into what you already have.
settings.sessionsStayNote: Nothing leaves this device unless you share it yourself.
settings.filesLocal: Your library and every session live in this app's own folder on this device. Nothing is uploaded and there's no account, so a backup is something you make rather than something that happens.
settings.filesInFilesApp: That folder is in the Files app: open Browse, look under this device's own storage, and Kettle is there — your library and every session are inside it, in a folder called exercise-tracker. Open exercises.yaml in a text editor, copy the folder to a computer, or send any file on from there. Copying it into iCloud Drive or Dropbox makes a snapshot rather than a live link: Kettle keeps writing here, so come back for a fresh copy.
settings.filesSync: Export sends exercises.yaml wherever you keep files — a cloud drive, a git repo, a mail to yourself. History exports the same way, one session at a time or the whole log as one file. Import merges a library back in by id, so a returning file updates only the items it names; a session log is exported for keeping and reading, not for importing.
settings.backupFolderNone: Not chosen yet. Pick a folder on this device.
settings.backupNowDetail: Write both files again straight away.
settings.backupForgetDetail: Kettle stops writing there and forgets where it was. The files already in the folder stay.
settings.backupUnsupported: Backing up to a folder isn't available on this device.
settings.backupUnreachable: That folder can't be reached any more. Choose it again.
settings.backupFolderNotSaved: That folder was chosen but couldn't be saved, so it won't be remembered after a restart.
settings.backupWhat: Kettle writes kettle-library.yaml and kettle-history.yaml into the folder you choose, at the end of every session and whenever you tap Back up now. It overwrites those two files and touches nothing else in there. Point it at a folder your sync app already watches and your log leaves the phone without Kettle ever sending anything.
settings.backupLimits: The library file can be imported back into a fresh install. The session log can't — Kettle exports it to keep and read, but has nothing that reads one back in, so treat it as a record rather than as a restore.

brief.prompt: This is the file format the Kettle workout app imports, and the ids already in my library. Reply with YAML matching the schema below. Reuse an existing id to replace that item; use a new id to add one. The app validates a few cross-field rules the schema can't express — if it refuses the file, it says why, and I'll paste that back to you.
